claim: The HLA region comprises just 0.3% of the genome yet contains 6.4% of the significant SNP associations in the EMBL-EBI genome wide association study (GWAS) catalog.
source: The HLA region is a well-known hotspot for disease associations: it comprises just 0.3% of the genome yet contains 6.4% of the significant SNP associations in the EMBL-EBI genome wide association study (GWAS) catalog (MacArthur et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to MacArthur et al., 2017, which provides the quantitative data about HLA region representation in GWAS catalogs.

claim: Multiple candidate gene and GWAS studies have identified significant associations between polymorphisms in the classical HLA class I genes and the risk and/or severity of infectious disease, a range of autoimmune conditions and a number of forms of cancer.
source: Multiple candidate gene and GWAS studies have identified significant associations between polymorphisms in the classical HLA class I genes and the risk and/or severity of infectious disease, a range of autoimmune conditions and a number of forms of cancer (Matzaraki et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matzaraki et al., 2017, which reviews HLA class I disease associations.

claim: A search of the literature yields over 2000 papers reporting HLA class I disease associations.
source: A search of the literature yields over 2000 papers reporting HLA class I disease associations.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' literature search, representing an inference from available published literature.

claim: The association between ankylosing spondylitis and possession of HLA-B*27 has an odds ratio greater than 100.
source: Some of the most striking odds of disease are seen with autoimmune conditions such as the association between ankylosing spondylitis and possession of HLA-B*27 (odds ratio >100) or between Behçet's Disease and HLA-B*51 (accounts for 32–50% of cases) (Matzaraki et al., 2017; de Menthon et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matzaraki et al., 2017 and de Menthon et al., 2009.

claim: HLA-B*51 accounts for 32–50% of Behçet's Disease cases.
source: Some of the most striking odds of disease are seen with autoimmune conditions such as the association between ankylosing spondylitis and possession of HLA-B*27 (odds ratio >100) or between Behçet's Disease and HLA-B*51 (accounts for 32–50% of cases) (Matzaraki et al., 2017; de Menthon et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matzaraki et al., 2017 and de Menthon et al., 2009.

claim: HLA-B*57 is strongly associated with reduced viral load and slow progression of disease in multiple HIV-1 cohorts.
source: HLA-B*57 is strongly associated with reduced viral load and slow progression of disease in multiple cohorts whilst HLA-B*35Px is associated with high viral load and poor prognosis (Pereyra et al., 2010; Carrington and O'Brien, 2003; Martin et al., 2007; Carrington et al., 1999; Kiepiela et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Pereyra et al., 2010; Carrington and O'Brien, 2003; Martin et al., 2007; Carrington et al., 1999; Kiepiela et al., 2004.

claim: HLA-B*35Px is associated with high viral load and poor prognosis in HIV-1 infection.
source: HLA-B*57 is strongly associated with reduced viral load and slow progression of disease in multiple cohorts whilst HLA-B*35Px is associated with high viral load and poor prognosis (Pereyra et al., 2010; Carrington and O'Brien, 2003; Martin et al., 2007; Carrington et al., 1999; Kiepiela et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Pereyra et al., 2010; Carrington and O'Brien, 2003; Martin et al., 2007; Carrington et al., 1999; Kiepiela et al., 2004.

claim: HLA class I molecules bind cytosolic peptides typically of length 8–11 amino acids.
source: the classical HLA class I molecules (HLA-A, -B and –C), which bind cytosolic peptides (typically of length 8–11 amino acids) have multiple functions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HLA class I molecule function.

claim: HLA class I molecules are ligands for several different receptors expressed by different immune cells including CD8+ T cells, NK cells and dendritic cells.
source: HLA class I molecules are the ligands for several different receptors expressed by different immune cells including CD8+ T cells, NK cells and dendritic cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HLA class I molecule function.

claim: The affinity of an HLA class I molecule for a peptide is a significant determinant of the CD8+ T cell response elicited by that peptide.
source: The affinity of an HLA class I molecule for a peptide is a significant determinant of the CD8+ T cell response elicited by that peptide (Chen et al., 2000; Müllbacher et al., 1999; Yewdell and Bennink, 1999; Deng et al., 1997; Boggiano et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Chen et al., 2000; Müllbacher et al., 1999; Yewdell and Bennink, 1999; Deng et al., 1997; Boggiano et al., 2005.

claim: 85% of epitopes bind their HLA molecule with an affinity of 500 nM or stronger.
source: it has been shown that 85% of epitopes bind their HLA molecule with an affinity of 500 nM or stronger (Assarsson et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Assarsson et al., 2007.

claim: 50–66% of peptides that bind HLA molecules do not elicit a CD8+ T cell response.
source: However the relationship between HLA binding and immunogenicity is nontrivial, 50–66% of peptides that bind do not elicit a response (Lee et al., 2004; Hoof et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2004 and Hoof et al., 2010.

claim: Cases where a peptide has undetectable HLA binding but still elicits a CD8+ T cell response have been described.
source: and conversely cases where a peptide has undetectable binding but still elicits a response have also been described (Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2004.

claim: Peptide positions P4-8 are most likely to be in close contact with the TCR.
source: It has been established that peptide positions P4-8 are most likely to be in close contact with the TCR (Rudolph et al., 2006; Garboczi et al., 1996; Calis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rudolph et al., 2006; Garboczi et al., 1996; Calis et al., 2012.

claim: Non-contact peptide positions can impact on TCR specificity.
source: However, which of these peptide positions are critical for a T cell's ability to bind have not been comprehensively mapped in humans; additionally non-contact positions can also impact on TCR specificity (Hausmann et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hausmann et al., 1999.

claim: A comprehensive study of murine data convincingly identified peptide positions P4-6 as important for TCR recognition.
source: A comprehensive study of murine data by the Kesmir group convincingly identified P4-6 (Calis et al., 2013) but it is unclear how this translates to human HLA:peptide as sparsity of data prevents a similar analysis in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Calis et al., 2013.

claim: KIRs are expressed mainly on the surface of NK cells and also some T cells.
source: KIRs are a family of inhibitory and activating receptors that are expressed mainly on the surface of NK cells and also some T cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about KIR expression.

claim: KIR2DL3 binds HLA-C molecules with a lysine at position 80 (designated the C1 group).
source: Whereas KIR2DL3 binds HLA-C molecules with a lysine at position 80 (designated the C1 group) (Trowsdale, 2001; Moesta et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Trowsdale, 2001 and Moesta et al., 2008.

claim: Exceptions to the broad KIR binding rules have been described.
source: Exceptions to these broad rules have been described (Sim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sim et al., 2017.

claim: KIR binding shows some dependence on the HLA-bound peptide, particularly positions 7 and 8.
source: KIR binding also shows some dependence on the HLA-bound peptide, particularly positions 7 and 8, though this specificity is weak compared to that of the TCR (Fadda et al., 2010; Maenaka et al., 1999a; Maenaka et al., 1999b; Boyington et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fadda et al., 2010; Maenaka et al., 1999a; Maenaka et al., 1999b; Boyington et al., 2000.

claim: The inhibitory CD94:NKG2A receptor ligates the monomorphic non-classical HLA-E loaded with peptide from the leader sequence of HLA-A, -C and a subset of –B molecules.
source: Particularly interesting is the inhibitory CD94:NKG2A receptor which ligates the monomorphic non-classical HLA-E loaded with peptide from the leader sequence of HLA-A, -C and a subset of –B molecules (Braud et al., 1998; López-Botet et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Braud et al., 1998 and López-Botet et al., 2000.

claim: CD94:NKG2A has been shown to play a key role in NK cell education.
source: and which has been recently shown to play a key role in NK cell education (Horowitz et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Horowitz et al., 2016.

claim: Different HLA allotypes bind LILRB1 and LILRB2 with varying affinity.
source: Different HLA allotypes bind LILRB1 and LILRB2 with varying affinity, this is particularly true for LILRB2 which shows considerable variation across the HLA alleles (Jones et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jones et al., 2011.

claim: LILRB1 and LILRB2 are inhibitory receptors expressed mainly on myeloid cells including dendritic cells and macrophages.
source: LILRB1 and LILRB2 are inhibitory receptors which are expressed mainly on myeloid cells including dendritic cells and macrophages
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about LILRB expression.

claim: Signalling via LILR affects the activation of antigen presenting cells.
source: signalling via LILR affects the activation of these antigen presenting cells (Bashirova et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bashirova et al., 2014.

claim: HLA-B*57 preferentially presents CD8+ T cell epitopes from the highly conserved Gag p24 protein which is less susceptible to escape mutations.
source: It has been suggested that HLA-B*57 is protective because it preferentially presents CD8+ T cell epitopes from the highly conserved Gag p24 protein which is less susceptible to escape mutations (Borghans et al., 2007; Kiepiela et al., 2007; Miura et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Borghans et al., 2007; Kiepiela et al., 2007; Miura et al., 2009.

claim: T cell responses to Gag are specifically associated with a reduced HIV-1 viral load.
source: and that T cell responses to Gag are specifically associated with a reduced HIV-1 viral load (Kiepiela et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kiepiela et al., 2007.

claim: The association between B*57 and low viral load is widely cited as evidence that CD8+ T cells are important in controlling HIV-1.
source: Indeed, the association between B*57 and low viral load is widely cited as evidence that CD8+ T cells are important in controlling HIV-1 (Boppana and Goepfert, 2018; Walker and McMichael, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boppana and Goepfert, 2018 and Walker and McMichael, 2012.

claim: It has been argued that HLA-B*57 is protective because of its role as a KIR ligand (binding both the inhibitory receptor KIR3DL1 and the activating receptor KIR3DS1).
source: However, it has also been argued (Flores-Villanueva et al., 2001) that HLA-B*57 is protective because of its role as a KIR ligand (binding both the inhibitory receptor KIR3DL1 and the activating receptor KIR3DS1); an argument which, though disputed (O'Brien et al., 2001), does appear to be supported by subsequent studies (Martin et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2002; Pelak et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Flores-Villanueva et al., 2001; O'Brien et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2002; Pelak et al., 2011.

claim: The unusually weak binding of HLA-B*57:01 for LILRB2 may contribute to control of HIV-1 viral load due to reduced inhibitory regulation of dendritic cells.
source: It has also been suggested that the unusually weak binding of HLA-B*57:01 for LILRB2 contributes to control of HIV-1 viral load due to its reduced inhibitory regulation of dendritic cells (Bashirova et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bashirova et al., 2014.

claim: HLA-B*57 provides peptides for HLA-E by virtue of having a methionine at position 21, thus supplying CD94:NKG2A ligands.
source: Finally, recent papers have called for a re-evaluation of HLA class I clinical associations, including HLA-B*57, taking into account the fact that HLA-B*57, by virtue of having a methionine at position 21 provides peptides for HLA-E thus supplying CD94:NKG2A ligands (Horowitz et al., 2016; Yunis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horowitz et al., 2016 and Yunis et al., 2007.

claim: For each of the four HLA class I alleles studied in HTLV-1 infection (A*02:06, A*02:07, C*08:01, B*54:01), TCR.FS was strongly associated with risk of disease in the same direction as the index allele.
source: We found that for each of the index HLA class I alleles considered, TCR.FS was strongly associated with risk of disease and in the same direction as the index allele i.e. possession of alleles with similar TCR binding to A*02:06, A*02:07 and C*08:01 are associated with a large decrease in the risk of disease whilst possession of alleles near B*54:01 in TCR binding space is associated with a significant increase in the risk of disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: In HTLV-1 infection, inclusion of TCR.FS in the multivariate analysis strengthened the effect of the index allele in every case.
source: In every case inclusion of TCR.FS in the multivariate analysis strengthened the effect of the index allele (i.e. increased the magnitude of the coefficient) indicating that removal of near alleles from the baseline made the 'background' alleles more dissimilar to the index.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: For all 4 HLA class I alleles studied in HTLV-1 infection, none of the metrics other than TCR.FS were significant.
source: None of the other metrics were significant for any of the index alleles considered.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: For all 4 HLA class I alleles studied in HTLV-1 infection, the protection/susceptibility associated with those alleles is best explained by their TCR binding properties and therefore is most likely to be attributable to CD8+ T cells.
source: We conclude that for all 4 HLA class I alleles studied in HTLV-1 infection the protection/susceptibility associated with those alleles is best explained by their TCR binding properties and therefore is most likely to be attributable to CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the regression analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: In HTLV-1 infection, there is a very strong positive correlation (Rs = + 0.76 p=5×10−6) between the protection conferred by an allele and the protection conferred by other alleles with similar TCR binding.
source: Across all alleles there was a very strong positive correlation between the protection conferred by an allele and the protection conferred by other alleles with similar TCR binding (Rs = + 0.76 p=5×10−6, Spearman Correlation two tailed).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis data presented in Figure 2 and the accompanying text.

claim: In HTLV-1 infection, in every case if the index allele was protective then alleles with similar TCR binding were also protective and if the index allele was detrimental then alleles with similar TCR binding were also detrimental (p=4×10−9).
source: 29 alleles were considered, in every case if the index was protective then alleles with similar TCR binding were also protective and if the index allele was detrimental then alleles with similar TCR binding were also detrimental (p=4×10−9, Binomial test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis data presented in the text.

claim: In HTLV-1 infection, no association was seen between protection/susceptibility and similarity by iKIR, aKIR, LILRB1, or LILRB2 metrics across all alleles.
source: No such association was seen for any of the other measures of similarity (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In HTLV-1 infection, when restricted to KIR binding alleles, a weak association was seen for iKIR (Rs = 0.6, p=0.07) but not for aKIR.
source: However, if we restricted the NK analysis to KIR binding alleles (ie. alleles with a C1, C2 or Bw4 motif) than a weak association was also seen for iKIR (Rs = 0.6, p=0.07, Spearman Correlation two tailed) but not for aKIR.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis data presented in the text.

claim: In HTLV-1 infection, the protection/susceptibility associated with an allele's nearest neighbours in CD8+ T cell recognition space was a significant determinant of protection/susceptibility (p=0.0006) even when all other metrics were included in the model.
source: The protection/susceptibility associated with an allele's nearest neighbours in CD8+ T cell recognition space was a significant determinant of protection/susceptibility (p=0.0006) even when all other metrics were included in the model.
evidence: This claim is supported by the multivariate regression analysis data.

claim: In HTLV-1 infection, the peptide:TCR binding properties of an allele is a significant determinant of the risk of disease associated with that allele for both extreme case alleles and intermediate 'average' alleles.
source: We conclude that, in HTLV-1 infection, the peptide:TCR binding properties of an allele is a significant determinant of the risk of disease associated with that allele; this is true not only for the extreme case alleles which are associated with significant protection or susceptibility but also for the intermediate 'average' alleles without significant associations.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the regression and correlation analysis data.

claim: In the HIV-1 cohort studied, HLA-B*35Px was associated with an increased viral load set point but did not have a significant impact on progression.
source: HLA-B*35Px was associated with an increased viral load set point but did not have a significant impact on progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the IAVI cohort data.

claim: In the HIV-1 cohort studied, HLA-B*57 was associated with a low early viral load set point and slow progression to low CD4 count.
source: HLA-B*57 was associated with a low early viral load set point and slow progression to low CD4 count.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the IAVI cohort data.

claim: In the HIV-1 cohort studied, the detrimental effect of B*35Px was entirely due to B*53:01 which was significantly associated with an increased early viral load set point.
source: The detrimental effect was entirely due to B*53:01 which was significantly associated with an increased early viral load set point, all other B*35Px alleles were infrequent in this cohort; (Appendix 3—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the IAVI cohort data presented in Appendix 3—table 2.

claim: HLA-B*53:01 is unusual in that its nearest allele out of all the 151 alleles in the HIV-1 cohort, in terms of both TCR and KIR recognition was distant (only 46% similarity).
source: HLA-B*53:01 is unusual in that its nearest allele out of all the 151 alleles in the cohort, in terms of both TCR and KIR recognition was distant (only 46% similarity).
evidence: This claim is based on the calculation of similarity metrics for the HIV-1 cohort.

claim: For B*53:01 in HIV-1 infection, alleles similar in terms of LILRB1 and LILRB2 binding had no significant impact on clinical outcome.
source: However, alleles similar to B*53:01 in terms of LILRB1 and LILRB2 binding behaved very differently in terms of their impact on clinical outcome: near alleles had no significant impact either on early viral load set point nor on time to low CD4+ cell count
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Table 2.

claim: The detrimental effects of B*53:01 in HIV-1 infection are independent of its LILRB binding properties.
source: We conclude that the detrimental effects of B*53:01 are independent of its LILRB binding properties but that we were not powered to study whether TCR or KIR binding effects were determinants of susceptibility.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the regression analysis data presented in Table 2.

claim: For the protective B*57 alleles in HIV-1 infection, alleles with similar aKIR binding to B*57:01, B*57:02 and B*57:03 were significantly protective.
source: We found a clear picture that alleles with similar aKIR binding to B*57:01, B*57:02 and B*57:03 were significantly protective (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Table 2.

claim: For the protective B*57 alleles in HIV-1 infection, there was a trend for alleles with similar TCR binding and similar LILRB2 binding to also be protective when these metrics were considered in isolation.
source: There was also a trend for alleles with similar TCR binding and similar LILRB2 binding to also be protective when these metrics were considered in isolation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Table 2.

claim: For the protective B*57 alleles in HIV-1 infection, when TCR and LILRB2 metrics were considered in a multivariate analysis with aKIR.FS, only aKIR.FS retained significance.
source: But when they were considered in a multivariate analysis with aKIR.FS only aKIR.FS retained significance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the multivariate regression analysis data.

claim: The main reason for the protective effect of HLA-B*57 in the HIV-1 cohort studied is attributable to its activating KIR binding properties.
source: We conclude that the main reason for the protective effect of HLA-B*57 in this cohort is attributable to its activating KIR binding properties.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the regression analysis data presented in Table 2.

claim: B*57:01, B*57:02 and B*57:03 all contain the Bw4-80I KIR binding motif and are thought to bind KIR3DS1.
source: B*57:01, B*57:02 and B*57:03 all contain the Bw4-80I KIR binding motif and are thought to bind KIR3DS1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HLA-B*57 alleles and their KIR binding properties.

claim: In the HIV-1 cohort studied, aKIR.FS was more protective (Coeff = −0.41 p=0.006) than KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I (Coeff = −0.22 p=0.04).
source: Interestingly, we found that aKIR.FS was more protective (Coeff = −0.41 p=0.006 **) than KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I (Coeff = −0.22 p=0.04 *).
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis comparing aKIR.FS and KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I.

claim: In the HIV-1 cohort studied, in a model including both aKIR.FS and KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I, aKIR.FS remained protective (Coeff = −0.52 p=0.07) whilst KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I lost significance and became detrimental (Coeff = +0.09, p=0.6).
source: And, in a model including both terms, aKIR.FS remained protective (Coeff = −0.52 p=0.07 .) whilst the compound genotype KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I loses significance and becomes, if anything, detrimental (Coeff = +0.09, p=0.6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the multivariate regression analysis data.

claim: aKIR.FS is a stronger determinant of protection in HIV-1 infection than KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I.
source: This indicates that though aKIR.FS and KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I are related, they are capturing slightly different features and that aKIR.FS is a stronger determinant of protection.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the regression analysis comparing aKIR.FS and KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I.

claim: In the HIV-1 cohort, individuals with KIR3DS1 and group I alleles (aKIR.FS >0.6) are strongly protected (Coeff = −0.4 p=0.007), an effect that is entirely dependent on the presence of KIR3DS1.
source: In particular people with KIR3DS1 and the group I alleles (aKIR.FS >0.6) are strongly protected; an effect that is entirely dependent on the presence of KIR3DS1 (group I allele with KIR3DS1 Coeff = −0.4 p=0.007 **; group I allele without KIR3DS1 Coeff = −0.05 p=0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Figure 3 and accompanying text.

claim: In the HIV-1 cohort, KIR3DS1 with group II or group III alleles offers no protection.
source: Whereas KIR3DS1 with the group II or group III alleles offers no protection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Figure 3 and accompanying text.

claim: In the HIV-1 cohort, amongst KIR3DS1− individuals, HLA-B*57:02 and B*57:03 both remained significantly protective (Coeff = −0.58 p=0.027, Coeff = −0.39 p=0.019).
source: HLA-B*57:02 and B*57:03 both remained significantly protective amongst KIR3DS1― individuals (Coeff = −0.58 p=0.027 *, Coeff = −0.39 p=0.019 *)
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data for KIR3DS1− individuals.

claim: Not all of the B*57:02 and B*57:03 protective effect in HIV-1 infection is attributable to their role as KIR3DS1 ligands.
source: indicating that not all of the B*57:02 and B*57:03 protective effect is attributable to their role as KIR3DS1 ligands.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the regression analysis data for KIR3DS1− individuals.

claim: In the HIV-1 cohort, amongst KIR3DS1− individuals, the best model to explain the residual protective effect of B*57:02 and B*57:03 was provided by their TCR binding.
source: Amongst KIR3DS1― individuals the best model to explain the residual protective effect of B*57:02 and B*57:03 was provided by their TCR binding, i.e. alleles with similar TCR binding were significantly protective (Appendix 3—table 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Appendix 3—table 5.

claim: HLA-B*57 alleles are protective in HIV-1 infection for two reasons: firstly (and most importantly) because of their activating KIR binding properties; secondly, their TCR binding properties.
source: We conclude that HLA-B*57 alleles are protective for two reasons: firstly (and most importantly) because of their activating KIR binding properties; secondly, their TCR binding properties.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the regression analysis data presented in Table 2 and Appendix 3—table 5.

claim: In HIV-1 infection, rank order of intermediate alleles was highly robust and significantly more informative than random (p<10−16).
source: We found that rank order of intermediate alleles was highly robust and significantly more informative than random (p<10−16 two sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test two-tailed) Appendix 2 Supplementary Results 'Are average HLA class I associations robust', Appendix 4—figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis data presented in Appendix 2 and Appendix 4—figure 2.

claim: In HIV-1 infection, no single interaction was able to explain all HLA associations across average alleles.
source: Unlike HTLV-1 infection, and more in line with expectation, the picture was mixed with no single interaction able to explain all HLA associations (Appendix 4—figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis data presented in Appendix 4—figure 3.

claim: In HIV-1 infection, the only significant correlation across average alleles was between the protection offered by an allele and the protection offered by alleles with similar LILRB2 binding (Rs = 0.29 p=0.048).
source: The only significant correlation was between the protection offered by an allele and the protection offered by alleles with similar LILRB2 binding. However, the correlation was weak (Rs = 0.29 p=0.048, Spearman two-tailed)
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis data.

claim: In HIV-1 infection, different interactions are responsible for the protection conferred by different HLA alleles.
source: We conclude that, in HIV-1 infection, different interactions are responsible for the protection conferred by different HLA alleles.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the correlation and regression analysis data.

claim: In the HCV cohort studied, the B*57 protective effect appeared to be attributable to B*57:02 (with B*57:03 and B*57:05 showing similar effects but not statistically significant due to low carrier numbers).
source: In the cohort we studied, the B*57 protective effect appeared to be attributable to B*57:02 (with B*57:03 and B*57:05 showing similar effects but were not statistically significant due to low carrier numbers); the more frequent B*57:01 allele did not appear to be protective (Appendix 3—table 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the HCV cohort data presented in Appendix 3—table 6.

claim: In the HCV cohort studied, the more frequent B*57:01 allele did not appear to be protective.
source: the more frequent B*57:01 allele did not appear to be protective (Appendix 3—table 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the HCV cohort data presented in Appendix 3—table 6.

claim: In HCV infection, there was no evidence that the aKIR-binding properties of the B*57 alleles contributed to their protection despite adequate power.
source: Unlike in HIV-1 infection, where the B*57 protective effect is mainly due to aKIR interactions, in HCV infection there was no evidence that the aKIR-binding properties of the B*57 alleles contributed to their protection (model 4 in Table 3 all the P values for aKIR.FS are very high, all the Coefficients are close to zero) despite adequate power.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Table 3.

claim: In HCV infection, the protective effect of B*57 alleles was explained by TCR.FS indicating that CD8+ T cells are most likely responsible.
source: Instead the protective effect was explained by TCR.FS (model 2) indicating that CD8+ T cells are most likely responsible for the protective effect of HLA-B*57 in HCV infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Table 3.

claim: In HCV infection, when covariates were omitted from the analysis, the finding that the protective effect was attributable to TCR.FS was strengthened.
source: We therefore repeated the analysis of models 1–6 omitting the covariates. This strengthened the finding that the protective effect was attributable to TCR.FS in every case leading to an increase in the size of the coefficient and a decrease in the P value (Coeff = 1.09, p=0.03 *, Coeff = 1.00 p=0.04 *, Coeff = 1.25 p=0.02* for TCR.FS with B*57:02, B*57:03 and B*57:05 respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data with and without covariates.

claim: In HCV infection, aKIR.FS never became significant even when covariates were omitted.
source: In contrast aKIR.FS never became significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data with and without covariates.

claim: In HCV infection, rank order of intermediate alleles was robust (p<10−16, 93.8% of runs significant).
source: Looking across all alleles, there was again substantial evidence that the rank order of protection conferred by average alleles was robust (p<10−16 two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test, 93.8% of runs significant, Appendix 2 Supplementary Results 'Are average HLA class I associations robust', Appendix 4—figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis data presented in Appendix 2 and Appendix 4—figure 2.

claim: In HCV infection, no single interaction was able to explain all HLA associations across average alleles.
source: As for HIV-1 infection, the picture was mixed with no single interaction able to explain all HLA associations (Appendix 4—figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis data presented in Appendix 4—figure 4.

claim: In HCV infection, the strongest positive correlation across average alleles was seen for alleles with similar TCR binding (Rs = 0.21 p=0.09), but the correlation is weak and not significant.
source: The strongest positive correlation was seen for alleles with similar TCR binding (Rs = 0.21 p=0.09, Spearman two-tailed) but the correlation is weak and not significant indicating that although the protection conferred by some alleles is attributable to TCR binding there are many alleles where the protection is better explained by another factor.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis data.

claim: The ancestral haplotype AH8.1 consists of HLA-A*01:01 -B*08:01- C*07:01 -DRB1*03:01 -DQA1*05:01 -DQB1*02:01.
source: The ancestral haplotype AH8.1 (also known as MHC 8.1) is a multigene haplotype consisting of HLA-A*01:01 -B*08:01- C*07:01 -DRB1*03:01 -DQA1*05:01 -DQB1*02:01.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of the AH8.1 haplotype.

claim: Genes from AH8.1 or the complete haplotype have been associated with risk or severity of disease in autoimmune hepatitis, myasthenia gravis, systemic lupus erythematosus, type 1 diabetes, a range of myositis phenotypes and Crohn's disease.
source: Genes from AH8.1 or the complete haplotype have been associated with risk or severity of disease in a number of inflammatory and autoimmune conditions including autoimmune hepatitis, myasthenia gravis, systemic lupus erythematosus, type 1 diabetes, a range of myositis phenotypes and Crohn's disease (Lee et al., 2017; Price et al., 1999; Manabe et al., 1993; Miller et al., 2015; Gorodezky et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2017; Price et al., 1999; Manabe et al., 1993; Miller et al., 2015; Gorodezky et al., 2006.

claim: In the Crohn's disease cohort studied, HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-C*07:01 (which are in tight linkage disequilibrium with each other and with the class II genes of the haplotype) but not HLA-A*01:01 were significantly associated with good prognosis.
source: In a cohort of 2650 Crohn's disease cases, HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-C*07:01 (which are in tight linkage disequilibrium with each other and with the class II genes of the haplotype) but not HLA-A*01:01 were significantly associated with good prognosis (Appendix 3—table 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the Crohn's disease cohort data presented in Appendix 3—table 7.

claim: In Crohn's disease, despite good power, alleles with similar TCR binding, similar iKIR binding, similar aKIR binding or similar LILRB1 and LILRB2 binding to either B*08:01 or C*07:01 were not associated with good prognosis.
source: Strikingly, despite good power in every case, we did not find that alleles with similar TCR binding, similar iKIR binding, similar aKIR binding or similar LILRB1 and LILRB2 binding to either B*08:01 or C*07:01 were associated with good prognosis (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Table 4.

claim: In Crohn's disease, for B*08:01 and C*07:01, the P values for all similarity metrics were very high and in some cases the direction of association was reversed (nearby alleles were detrimental).
source: The results were very clear, in every case the P values were very high and in some cases the direction of association was if, anything, reversed (nearby alleles were detrimental).
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis data presented in Table 4.

claim: The protection marked by B*08:01 and C*07:01 in Crohn's disease is either attributable to other genes in the extended haplotype or B*08:01 and C*07:01 confer protection by a mechanism other than immune receptor binding.
source: This suggests that the protection marked by B*08:01 and C*07:01 is either attributable to other genes in this extended haplotype or that B*08:01 and C*07:01 confer protection by a mechanism other than immune receptor binding (Elahi et al., 2011; Candore et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the regression analysis data presented in Table 4, with supporting citations to Elahi et al., 2011 and Candore et al., 1995.

claim: The AH8.1 haplotype is associated with impaired immune activation, perhaps due to a defect in the TCR signal transduction pathway.
source: A number of studies have reported that the AH8.1 haplotype is associated with impaired immune activation, perhaps due to a defect in the TCR signal transduction pathway (Candore et al., 1995; Lio et al., 1995; Egea et al., 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Candore et al., 1995; Lio et al., 1995; Egea et al., 1991.

claim: In HIV-1 infection, all the B*57 alleles with high carrier frequency (B*57:01, B*57:02, B*57:03) are associated with protection both in the cohort studied and in the work of others.
source: It is interesting to note that in HIV-1 infection all the B*57 alleles with high carrier frequency (B*57:01, B*57:02, B*57:03) are associated with protection both in the cohort we study and in the work of others (Carrington and O'Brien, 2003; Kiepiela et al., 2004; Costello et al., 1999; Fellay et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the HIV-1 cohort data and citations to Carrington and O'Brien, 2003; Kiepiela et al., 2004; Costello et al., 1999; Fellay et al., 2007.

claim: In HCV infection, B*57:02 and B*57:03 are protective, but the evidence for B*57:01-mediated protection is less clear.
source: However, in HCV infection, B*57:02 and B*57:03 are protective, but the evidence for B*57:01-mediated protection is less clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the HCV cohort data.

claim: B*57:01 is not significantly protective in the HCV cohort studied despite a large number of carriers.
source: B*57:01 is not significantly protective in the cohort we study despite a large number of carriers
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the HCV cohort data.

claim: For the HIV-1 proteome, all the B*57 alleles are very similar (e.g. when the index is B*57:02 the TCR.FS with B*57:01 is 0.74).
source: For the HIV-1 proteome, all the B*57 alleles are very similar (e.g. when the index is B*57:02 the TCR.FS with B*57:01 is 0.74 and only 2 alleles –B*58:02 and B*57:03- are more similar).
evidence: This claim is based on the calculation of TCR.FS metrics for the HIV-1 proteome.

claim: For HCV, whilst B*57:02 and B*57:03 are similar, B*57:01 is more distant (e.g. when the index is B*57:02 the TCR.FS with B*57:01 drops to 0.58 and 10 alleles are more similar to B*57:02 than B*57:01).
source: In contrast for HCV, whilst B*57:02 and B*57:03 are similar, B*57:01 is more distant (e.g. when the index is B*57:02 the TCR.FS with B*57:01 drops to 0.58 and 10 alleles are more similar to B*57:02 than B*57:01).
evidence: This claim is based on the calculation of TCR.FS metrics for the HCV proteome.

claim: The difference in TCR.FS between B*57 alleles for HIV-1 versus HCV proteomes provides a plausible explanation for why B*57:01 confers similar protection to B*57:02 and B*57:03 in HIV-1 but appears to have less similarity in HCV infection.
source: This provides a plausible explanation for why B*57:01 confers a similar degree of protection to B*57:02 and B*57:03 in the context of HIV-1 infection but appears to have less similarity in the context of HCV infection.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the TCR.FS calculations for different proteomes.

claim: For all three viral infections studied, the rank order of 'average' alleles was robust.
source: Another interesting observation was that, for all three viral infections, the rank order of 'average' alleles was robust, that is, they could be robustly classified as protective or detrimental.
evidence: This claim is supported by the subsampling analysis data presented in Appendix 2 and Appendix 4—figure 2.

claim: The TCR.FS metric finds that alleles within the same supertype are more similar than alleles between supertypes (p=3×10−7).
source: Firstly, the TCR.FS metric finds that alleles within the same supertype are more similar (have a higher TCR.FS) than alleles between supertypes (p=3×10−7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the validation analysis data presented in Appendix 2 and Appendix 4—figure 1.

claim: For HTLV-1 infection, there is a very strong positive correlation between the risk of HAM/TSP associated with an allele and the risk of HAM/TSP associated with similar alleles by the TCR.FS metric.
source: Secondly, for HTLV-1 infection we find a very strong positive correlation between the risk of HAM/TSP associated with an allele and the risk of HAM/TSP associated with similar alleles (by the TCR.FS metric).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In HIV-1 infection, similarity in terms of activating KIR binding (aKIR.FS) revealed clinically relevant subtleties lost within the traditional KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I protective group, splitting this group into 3 groups with decreasing levels of protection.
source: Thirdly, in HIV-1 infection we found that similarity in terms of activating KIR binding (aKIR.FS) revealed clinically relevant subtleties lost within the traditional KIR3DS1:Bw4-80I protective group, essentially splitting this group into 3 groups with decreasing levels of protection
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis data presented in Figure 3.

claim: This method should not be used in isolation as the sole method for determining the mechanism underlying an HLA association.
source: We stress that this method should not be used in isolation as the sole method for determining the mechanism underlying an HLA association.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation from the authors.

claim: This method should be used alongside other lines of evidence to triangulate to the most likely answer.
source: Rather it provides a line of evidence to be used alongside other lines of evidence to triangulate to the most likely answer.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation from the authors.

claim: Many of the problems arising in classical HLA disease association studies, such as linkage disequilibrium, unmeasured confounding variables or population stratification are less of a problem with these metrics.
source: In common with classical disease association approaches (which use HLA alleles as predictors), this method should be used with care. Many of the problems arising in classical HLA disease association studies, such as linkage disequilibrium, unmeasured confounding variables or population stratification are less of a problem with these metrics.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the method based on its design.

claim: Many alleles will be similar and contribute to the similarity metric and it is unlikely that all similar alleles will all be in linkage disequilibrium with the same polymorphism or all correlated with the same confounder.
source: This is because many alleles will be similar and contribute to the similarity metric and it is unlikely that all similar alleles will all be in linkage disequilibrium with the same polymorphism or all correlated with the same confounder.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the method based on its design.

claim: Linkage disequilibrium and other correlations can and will distort the results and should be investigated.
source: Nevertheless linkage disequilibrium and other correlations can and will distort the results and should be investigated.
evidence: This is a methodological caution from the authors.

claim: The method should be used with care by someone with knowledge both of the biological problem and the structure of the dataset.
source: In short, the method should not be used blindly, it should be used with care by someone with knowledge both of the biological problem and the structure of the dataset.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation from the authors.

claim: A limitation of this approach is the relatively simple definition of the KIR binding groups which does not take into account the KIR allele or variations in KIR-HLA binding that break the C1/C2 and Bw4/Bw6 rules.
source: Another limitation of this approach is the relatively simple definition of the KIR binding groups which does not take into account the KIR allele or variations in KIR-HLA binding that break the C1/C2 and Bw4/Bw6 rules.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation.

claim: Simplistic KIR binding groupings have proved very powerful in other studies, indicating that, to a first approximation, they are informative.
source: Nevertheless, these simplistic groupings have proved very powerful in other studies (Martin et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2002; Pelak et al., 2011; Vince et al., 2014; Khakoo et al., 2004; Ahlenstiel et al., 2008; Nakimuli et al., 2015), indicating that, to a first approximation, they are informative.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Martin et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2002; Pelak et al., 2011; Vince et al., 2014; Khakoo et al., 2004; Ahlenstiel et al., 2008; Nakimuli et al., 2015.

claim: The study does not investigate all known receptor-HLA interactions; instead it focuses on receptor-ligand pairs which are polymorphic and well-characterised.
source: We do not study all known receptor-HLA interactions; instead we focus on receptor-ligand pairs which are polymorphic and well-characterised.
evidence: This is a description of the scope of the study.

claim: The study investigates TCR-HLA:peptide, inhibitory KIR-HLA:peptide, activating KIR-HLA:peptide, LILRB1-HLA and LILRB2-HLA interactions.
source: Specifically we investigate TCR-HLA:peptide, inhibitory KIR-HLA:peptide, activating KIR-HLA:peptide, LILRB1-HLA and LILRB2-HLA.
evidence: This is a description of the scope of the study.

claim: The study did not investigate the CD94:NKG2A-HLA interaction since, with current knowledge, alleles could only be split in a binary fashion into binders or non-binders which would provide no power in subsequent analysis.
source: In particular we did not investigate the CD94:NKG2A-HLA interaction since, with current knowledge, we could only split alleles in a binary fashion into binders or non-binders which would provide no power in subsequent analysis.
evidence: This is an explanation of a methodological limitation.

claim: The strength of CD94:NKG2A-HLA binding is known to be more subtle than binary and to depend on the peptide interaction with both CD94 and NKG2A, but there is no comprehensive data to allow characterisation of this binding.
source: The strength of binding is known to be more subtle than this and to depend on the peptide interaction with both CD94 and NKG2A (Petrie et al., 2008) but there is no comprehensive data to allow us to characterise this binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Petrie et al., 2008 and acknowledges a data limitation.

claim: The study does not investigate atypical effects of the HLA molecules.
source: We do not study atypical effects of the HLA molecules (Elahi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the scope of the study with a citation to Elahi et al., 2011.

claim: Monomorphic receptor-ligand pairs are not studied as these cannot explain polymorphic HLA associations.
source: Monomorphic receptor-ligand pairs are not studied as these cannot explain polymorphic HLA associations.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the scope of the study.

claim: This approach could be used alongside classical GWAS or candidate gene approaches as a tool for investigating identified HLA associations.
source: In addition to identifying immune interactions underlying HLA class I disease associations this approach could also be used alongside classical GWAS or candidate gene approaches as a tool for investigating identified HLA associations.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future applications of the method.

claim: Lack of association between 'near' alleles and outcome may indicate that the identified allele is a passenger marking the causal variant or a false positive.
source: Lack of association between 'near' alleles and outcome may indicated that the identified allele is a passenger marking the causal variant or a false positive.
evidence: This is a suggestion for interpreting results from the method.

claim: Raychaudhuri et al. extended the usual approach of identifying alleles associated with disease traits and instead fine mapped associations down to the level of amino acids.
source: Raychaudrhuri et al extended the usual approach of identifying alleles associated with disease traits and instead fine mapped associations down to the level of amino acids.
evidence: This claim describes the work of Raychaudhuri et al. (2012).

claim: Raychaudhuri et al. identified 5 amino acids, all in the peptide binding grove of HLA molecules, that were associated with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis.
source: This high resolution approach identified 5 amino acids, all in the peptide binding grove of HLA molecules, that were associated with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis.
evidence: This claim describes the findings of Raychaudhuri et al. (2012).

claim: Raychaudhuri et al. assumed that variation in the CD8+ T cell response elicited must explain the observed associations.
source: However, the authors assumed that variation in the CD8+ T cell response elicited must explain the observed associations.
evidence: This claim describes an assumption made by Raychaudhuri et al. (2012).

claim: Genetic association studies provide a rare and powerful opportunity to uncover causal factors in human disease.
source: Studies of human disease are typically observational and correlative in nature. An exception to this is genetic association studies which provide a rare and powerful opportunity to uncover causal factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the value of genetic association studies.

claim: Knowing the causal factors will lead to a better understanding of the molecular pathways involved in disease pathogenesis and help to identify potential therapeutic targets.
source: Ultimately, knowing the causal factors will lead to a better understanding of the molecular pathways involved in disease pathogenesis and help to identify potential therapeutic targets.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the value of understanding causal factors.

claim: NetMHCpan version 4.0 was used to predict the peptides bound by a given HLA class I molecule.
source: NetMHCpan version 4.0 was used to predict the peptides bound by a given HLA class I molecule.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: A percentile rank of 2% was used as the threshold for bound peptides with peptides below this rank being considered to be bound.
source: A percentile rank of 2% was used as the threshold for bound peptides with peptides below this rank being considered to be bound (Nielsen et al., 2007; Jurtz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study with supporting citations.

source: For HTLV-1, the subjects were from Kagoshima and so the HTLV-1 subtype prevalent in Japan was used (Uniprot accession: J02029).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: For HIV-1 (IAVI cohort from East and South Africa), Zambian HIV-C subtype was used (Uniprot accession: AB254142).
source: For IAVI (subjects from East and South Africa), Zambian HIV-C subtype was used (Uniprot accession: AB254142).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

source: For HCV (subjects from US and UK) HCV subtype 1a was used (Uniprot Accession: M62321).

claim: For Crohn's Disease 100 random human proteins were used.
source: For Crohn's Disease 100 random human proteins were used.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

source: For small proteomes (e.g. the viral proteomes considered here which were all less than 5000 amino acids) then results differ depending on the choice of proteome (e.g. alleles which are similar in terms of binding to HCV are not necessarily similar in terms of binding to HIV-1)
evidence: This is an observation about the properties of the method.

claim: Once the proteome becomes large, the exact choice of proteome does not impact the results.
source: but once the proteome becomes large, then the exact choice of proteome does not impact the results.
evidence: This is an observation about the properties of the method.

claim: The HTLV-1 cohort consists of 392 HTLV-1-infected individuals from Kagoshima in Southern Japan.
source: We studied a case-control cohort of 392 HTLV-1-infected individuals from Kagoshima in Southern Japan.
evidence: This is a description of the cohort used in the study.

claim: In the HTLV-1 cohort, 178 subjects were asymptomatic carriers of the virus, and 214 subjects were diagnosed with HAM/TSP.
source: 178 subjects were asymptomatic carriers of the virus, and 214 subjects were diagnosed with HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP) according to World Health Organisation criteria.
evidence: This is a description of the cohort used in the study.

claim: There are well-documented associations between HLA-A*02, HLA-C*08 and HLA-B*54 and outcome in HTLV-1 infection.
source: There are well-documented associations between HLA-A*02, HLA-C*08 and HLA-B*54 and outcome (Jeffery et al., 1999; Jeffery et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jeffery et al., 1999 and Jeffery et al., 2000.

claim: HLA-A*02 and HLA-C*08 are protective in HTLV-1 infection: they are associated with a reduced risk of HAM/TSP.
source: HLA-A*02 and HLA-C*08 are protective: they are associated with a reduced risk of HAM/TSP
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the HTLV-1 cohort data.

claim: HLA-B*54 is detrimental in HTLV-1 infection: it is associated with an increased risk of HAM/TSP.
source: whilst HLA-B*54 is detrimental: it is associated with an increased risk of HAM/TSP.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the HTLV-1 cohort data.

claim: In the HTLV-1 cohort, A*02:06 and A*02:07 are associated with a reduced risk of disease.
source: A*02:06 and A*02:07 are associated with a reduced risk of disease
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the HTLV-1 cohort data presented in Appendix 3—table 1.

claim: In the HTLV-1 cohort, C*08:01 was weakly associated with a reduced risk of disease.
source: C*08:01 was weakly associated with a reduced risk of disease
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the HTLV-1 cohort data presented in Appendix 3—table 1.

claim: In the HTLV-1 cohort, B*54:01 was associated with an increased risk of disease.
source: and B*54:01 was associated with an increased risk of disease (Appendix 3—table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the HTLV-1 cohort data presented in Appendix 3—table 1.

source: IAVI is a prospective cohort of HIV-1 seroconverters who were identified when seronegative and followed under Protocol C of IAVI (International AIDS Vaccine Initiative, 2020).

source: The IAVI cohort consisted of N = 568 individuals with time to low CD4 count information and N = 524 individuals with early viral load information.

source: The HCV cohort consists of four sub-cohorts of HCV-seropositive subjects: AIDS Link to Intravenous Experience (ALIVE, N = 226) (Vlahov et al., 1991), Multicenter Hemophilia Cohort Study (MHCS, N = 295) (Goedert et al., 1989), Hemophilia Growth and Development Study (HGDS, N = 100) (Hilgartner et al., 1993) and a UK cohort (N = 161) (Khakoo et al., 2004; Seich Al Basatena et al., 2011; Boelen et al., 2018).

claim: The Crohn's disease cohort consists of 788 poor-prognosis cases and 1424 good-prognosis cases.
source: The Crohn's disease cohort consists of two, previously reported cohorts of Crohn's disease cases (a total of 788 poor-prognosis cases and 1424 good-prognosis cases) (Lee et al., 2017; Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium, 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the cohort used in the study with supporting citations.
